title: Lazarus: Why Did Jesus Wait?
paragraphs: Lazarus: Why Did Jesus Wait?

Jesus was not late.
He was deliberate.
That is the part your pain struggles to believe.
Because when Lazarus got sick, Jesus did not rush. He did not sprint to Bethany. He did not send immediate relief. He did not heal him from a distance, though He had done that before. He waited.
And Lazarus died.
Read that again.

He waited.
And Lazarus died.

For the broken, that sounds cruel at first. Because you know what it feels like to pray and hear nothing. To beg God to move and watch the situation get worse. To ask for healing, rescue, restoration, and instead watch the door close, the body weaken, the relationship collapse, the opportunity rot in front of you.

You prayed.
God saw it.
You cried.
God saw it.
You thought He would come sooner.
You knew.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus sometimes delays what you want because He is preparing something greater than what you asked for.

In John 11:3–6, the sisters sent word to Jesus:
“Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.”
And after hearing it, Jesus said:
“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.”
Then Scripture says something shocking:
“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.”
Did you catch that?

Not although He loved them.
Because He loved them, He waited.
That destroys the lie that delay always means abandonment.

Sometimes the silence of God is not rejection.
Sometimes it is positioning.
Sometimes it is holy restraint.
Sometimes Jesus will let a situation pass the point of human fixing so that when He moves, no one can confuse His power with human effort.
That is where many of you are fighting God.

You do not just want His help.
You want His help on your schedule.
You want divine power, but under your terms.
You want resurrection without death.
Victory without surrender.
Glory without brokenness.
But that is not how Jesus works.

He does not merely improve dead things.
He raises them.
And before He raises them, He often lets everyone discover that they are truly dead.

That is not just Lazarus’ story.
That is yours.

Your sin was not “sickness” that needed a little moral treatment.
It was death.

Ephesians 2:1 says,
“And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.”

Dead. Not wounded.
Dead. Not struggling a little.
Dead in sin.
Separated from God.
Unable to save yourself.
Unable to clean yourself up enough for heaven.
That is the spiritual diagnosis.

You were not waiting for advice.
You were waiting for resurrection.
And that is why the Lazarus story is bigger than a funeral. It is a mirror.

Martha and Mary thought the crisis was sickness.
Jesus knew the deeper issue was revelation.

They wanted healing.
Jesus intended glory.

They wanted intervention before death.
Jesus planned to reveal Himself after death.
Because there is something about a sealed tomb that exposes what people truly believe.
When Jesus finally arrived, Martha met Him with the sentence many people still carry in their hearts:
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” — John 11:21
That is the cry of disappointed faith.
“Lord, if You had acted sooner…”

If You had answered that prayer sooner.
If You had saved that marriage sooner.
If You had stopped that addiction sooner.
If You had healed that body sooner.
If You had opened that door sooner.
That is where heartbreak becomes accusation.

But Jesus did not answer Martha with an apology.
He answered her with Himself.
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” — John 11:25

Not, “I know resurrection.”
Not, “I can teach on life.”
Not, “I can improve outcomes.”
“I am.”
This is the center.

Jesus did not come merely to solve one family’s tragedy.
He came to reveal that He is the only Lord over death, sin, judgment, and the grave.
And this is where the Gospel turns sharp.

Because many people want Jesus as comfort, but not as Lord.
As helper, but not as King.
As emotional support, but not as Savior from sin.
You want Him near enough to soothe you, but not holy enough to confront you.

But Jesus does not step into Bethany to offer sentimental words.
He steps in as the Son of God who commands the grave.
And before He speaks to Lazarus, He tells them something uncomfortable:
“Take ye away the stone.” — John 11:39

Martha resists:
“Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.”
There it is.
Exposure.

By now, it smells.
By now, it is undeniable.
By now, nobody can pretend it is not gone.

That is what many of you fear spiritually. You do not want the stone moved because you know what is behind it. Secret sin. Hypocrisy. pornography. pride. bitterness. unbelief. religious performance. hidden compromise. The image you protected. The rot you managed. The tomb you decorated.

God saw it.
You knew.
And still you hoped maybe Jesus would bless the outside without opening the inside.
He will not.
He loves too deeply to leave the stone in place.

Because grace is not denial.
Grace is resurrection truth breaking into the place you stopped hoping.
Then Jesus prays, lifts His eyes, and cries with a loud voice:
“Lazarus, come forth.” — John 11:43
And the dead man came out.

Bound hand and foot.
Face wrapped.
Alive, but still carrying grave clothes.
That is another word for somebody right now.
Jesus can bring you out of death in an instant, but sanctification is the process of taking off what belonged to your grave.

Saved, but still learning.
Alive, but still being unbound.
Free in Christ, but still shedding what your old life wrapped around you.
That is why salvation is not behavior modification. It is new life in Jesus Christ.
And how do you receive that life?

Not by works.
Not by trying harder.
Not by religious performance.
Not by pretending you are not dead.

Ephesians 2:8–9 says,
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
This is the Gospel:

You sinned against a holy God.
Your sin deserved judgment.
You could not save yourself.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, lived without sin, died on the cross for sinners, and rose again in victory.
He took the punishment sin deserved.
He offers mercy, forgiveness, and eternal life to all who repent and believe.
That means the deepest reason Jesus waited at Lazarus’ tomb points beyond Bethany to Calvary.
Because soon, Jesus Himself would be laid in a tomb.
But unlike Lazarus, Jesus did not die because sickness touched Him. He died because He willingly took the place of sinners. And unlike Lazarus, Jesus rose never to die again.

Lazarus was a sign.
Jesus is the Savior.

Lazarus came out still needing others to loose him.
Jesus rose in total triumph, having crushed death itself.

Romans 5:8 says,
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

And 1 Corinthians 15:55–57 declares,
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? ... thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
So why did Jesus wait?

He waited to reveal that His love is deeper than immediate relief.
He waited to reveal that faith must rest in who He is, not only in what He does.
He waited to reveal that when human hope is buried, divine glory can still speak.
He waited to show that He is not merely a healer of the sick, but the resurrection of the dead.
And maybe that is why He has allowed certain things in your life to reach the point where your strength failed.

Not because He is absent.
Not because He is powerless.
Not because He is cruel.

But because He is bringing you to the end of yourself, where you stop trusting your ability, your goodness, your religion, your excuses, and finally fall before the only One who can call dead things to live.
This is your decision moment.

Stop accusing God for not serving your timeline.
Stop dressing up a tomb and calling it life.
Stop hiding behind delay as an excuse for unbelief.
Repent.

Turn from sin.
Turn from self.
Turn from dead religion.
Turn to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest miracle in the Lazarus story is not that one man came out of a tomb.
It is that the same Christ still speaks life to the spiritually dead.

And when He calls, you do not negotiate.
You come out.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
But Jesus is still writing stories where graves become testimonies.

So hear the voice behind the tears.
Hear the authority behind the silence.
Hear the Christ who waited, not to destroy hope, but to redefine it.

The tomb is not bigger than Jesus.
Your sin is not deeper than His mercy.
Your delay is not stronger than His purpose.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

The question was never only, “Why did Jesus wait?”
The real question is:
When He calls your name, will you come out?
Read that again.
